title: Polymer clay stamped gift tags
subtitle: A set of six marbled polymer clay gift tags stamped with botanical impressions and fitted with cord loops
excerpt: Polymer clay gift tags are small rectangular or oval clay pieces stamped with botanical impression stamps and baked in a domestic oven at 110-130°C. No kiln is required. A set of six tags is made from one 50 g block of marbled polymer clay, each fitted with a jute or cotton cord loop.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles for polymer clay jewellery and paper-craft hybrid work.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that sets hard in a domestic oven at 110-130°C; decorative only, not food-safe
Warming and kneading polymer clay by hand until soft and pliable, preventing cracking after baking
Partially blending two or more colours of polymer clay together to create a swirled pattern without fully mixing them
Pressing a raised or textured stamp into soft clay to transfer the pattern as a recessed impression in the clay surface

content.text: Polymer clay gift tags are small clay pieces stamped with botanical impressions and baked in a domestic oven, not a kiln.
Polymer clay

sets at 110-130°C and produces a durable, lightweight tag that will not tear or soften in damp conditions like paper tags do. A set of six tags uses 50 g of marbled clay and bakes in one tray, fitted with cord loops after cooling.

materials.name: Polymer clay, two colours for marbling (e.g. cream and sage green, or white and terracotta)
Jute, cotton, or waxed linen cord for loops, cut into 15 cm lengths
Acrylic paint, one colour (for filling the stamped impression to make it readable)

tools.name: Pottery rolling pin (or smooth glass bottle)
Fettling knife or craft knife (for cutting tag shapes)

content.text: Preparation

Botanical impression stamps for polymer clay include rubber stamps, carved wooden stamps, or real botanical material (fern fronds, seed heads, leaves with pronounced veining). All of these transfer a clear impression into soft polymer clay. Do not use paper or card as stamps: these stick to the raw clay surface. Work on a smooth tile or a sheet of glass so the clay sheet releases cleanly. Decide on your tag shape before starting: rectangular (4 cm x 6 cm), oval (3.5 cm x 5.5 cm), or an arch top are all classic gift-tag formats.
Conditioning and marbling
Condition
each colour separately: knead 25 g of each colour between your palms for two minutes until warm and smooth. The clay stretches without tearing when conditioned.
To
marble

the two colours, roll each into a 12 cm log. Lay the logs side by side and twist them together three or four times. Fold the twist in half, roll out again, and twist once more. Stop at four or five repeats to keep distinct colour swirls.
Roll the marbled clay into a ball, then flatten and roll to a sheet 4 mm thick on your tile. The sheet should be large enough to cut six tags: roughly 15 cm x 20 cm.
Stamping the impressions
Impression stamp

the sheet before cutting the individual tags: it is easier to stamp a flat sheet than individual small pieces. Press the botanical stamp firmly into the clay surface at a 90-degree angle and lift straight back up. Do not rock the stamp sideways, which blurs the impression.

Space the impressions across the sheet so each tag will have at least one motif clearly visible within its outline. A fern frond impression, a leaf impression, or a seed head impression centred on the tag face works well.

For real botanical material: lay the leaf or fern face-down on the clay sheet, roll the rolling pin over it once with firm pressure, then peel away. The vein pattern transfers as a recessed impression.
Cutting the tags and piercing cord holes

Cut paper templates for your chosen tag shape. Lay each template on the stamped sheet so the motif sits within the tag outline. Cut around each template with the fettling knife in clean single strokes.

Pierce a cord hole at the narrow end of each tag with the needle tool: 3 mm in diameter, placed 5 mm from the edge. For rectangular tags, the hole sits at the centre of one short edge. For oval tags, it sits at the most pointed end.
Transfer all six tags on baking parchment to a flat oven tray. Ensure the tags are lying perfectly flat: any curve baked in is permanent.
Baking
Bake at 110-130°C (conventional oven, not fan) for 20 minutes. Thin pieces like these cure faster than thick sculpted forms. Allow to cool completely before handling.
Finishing

Once cool, highlight the stamped impression if desired: apply a thin coat of acrylic paint in a contrasting colour across the whole face, then immediately wipe away the surface paint with a dry cloth. Paint remains in the recessed impression lines and is wiped clean from the raised surfaces, creating a two-tone effect. Once the paint is dry, seal the entire tag with a coat of matte acrylic varnish. Thread a 15 cm length of cord through each hole and tie in a knot to form the hanging loop.
Care

Baked polymer clay is water-resistant and does not tear like paper tags. The cord loop can be retied when moving a gift tag from one package to another. Store unused tags in a flat box away from direct sunlight. The acrylic varnish layer protects the painted highlights from rubbing off.
Variations

Use a single-colour clay rather than marbled for a cleaner look, and fill the stamped impressions with gold or copper paint to make the botanical motif stand out. White clay with gold impressions looks particularly striking as a gift tag on a dark-paper parcel.
Make a mixed set: cut some tags in rectangular format and some in oval format from the same marbled sheet for visual variety in a set of six.

Write directly on the tag surface with a paint pen or a fine permanent marker after the varnish coat: polymer clay provides a more stable writing surface than paper. The writing stays legible and does not bleed.

items.problem: Tags curved upward in the oven during baking
items.cause: Tags were placed on a slightly uneven tray, or the clay was not fully flat before baking
items.fix: Bake on a flat ceramic tile or the back of a flat oven tray. If already curved, reheat for 5 minutes, then immediately press flat between two tiles and allow to cool under pressure

items.problem: Stamped impression too faint to see
items.cause: Insufficient pressure when stamping, or the clay was too cold and resistant
items.fix: Condition the clay more thoroughly before rolling and stamping. Press the stamp firmly with both hands for 5 seconds rather than a single glancing press. Highlighting the impression with paint after baking makes a faint impression legible

items.problem: Cord hole cracked at the edges after baking
items.cause: Hole was placed too close to the edge; less than 5 mm of clay at the edge is not enough to withstand the pull of a cord
items.fix: Place holes at least 5 mm from the edge. After baking, use a 2 mm hand drill to carefully enlarge a cracked hole back to a clean circle, then seal the crack with a drop of superglue

items.problem: Marbled colours fully blended into one flat colour
items.cause: Too many twists when marbling; polymer clay blends fully with repeated working
items.fix: Stop at four or five folds. If the colours have blended flat, use the solid colour and add visual interest through the stamp impression and paint highlighting instead
